mechanism_narrative: WORKPLACES mobility has risen monotonically from -20.6% to -11.7% over four weeks, signaling workplace return. This trend will continue, driving commuter retail spending and lifting RETAIL_REC over the next four weeks.
evidence_refs: fact:WORKPLACES improved 8.9 percentage points over four weeks
failure_condition: RETAIL_REC mean over next 28 days is not higher than the mean over the last 28 days, or WORKPLACES reverses direction (falls below -11.7%) in week t+1.

mechanism_narrative: GROCERY_PHARM has stabilized at +20.4% (range 19.9–21.0%), indicating sustained essential-goods purchasing. This behavioral lock-in will suppress discretionary retail spending, keeping RETAIL_REC depressed over the next four weeks.
evidence_refs: fact:GROCERY_PHARM variance <1.1 percentage points over four weeks
failure_condition: RETAIL_REC rises above -10% in the next four weeks while GROCERY_PHARM remains above +19%.

mechanism_narrative: TRANSIT mobility remains suppressed (range -2.9 to -0.4%), constraining commuter access to retail districts. If TRANSIT falls below -3% in week t+1, retail footfall will contract further, driving RETAIL_REC lower over the next four weeks.
candidate_trigger: TRANSIT falls below -3.0% in any single week
evidence_refs: fact:TRANSIT has not exceeded -0.4% in four weeks
failure_condition: RETAIL_REC increases by more than 2 percentage points over the next 14 days despite TRANSIT falling below -3%.

mechanism_narrative: RESIDENTIAL mobility remains elevated at +5.0%, and PARKS mobility is suppressed at -19.9%. This combination signals holiday-season indoor confinement behavior. As December progresses toward year-end, retail-and-recreation venues will see increased foot traffic for holiday shopping, reversing the current -13.3% deficit.
evidence_refs: fact:RESIDENTIAL stable at +5.0–5.3%, PARKS stable at -19.9 to -21.3%
failure_condition: RETAIL_REC does not rise above -10% by week t+4, or PARKS mobility does not improve (rise) by at least 3 percentage points.

mechanism_narrative: WORKPLACES recovery (+8.9 points over four weeks) combined with stable GROCERY_PHARM (+20.4%) indicates bifurcated mobility: workers returning but essential-goods substitution persisting. This interaction suppresses discretionary retail, keeping RETAIL_REC negative over the next four weeks.
failure_condition: RETAIL_REC rises above -8% over the next 28 days while both WORKPLACES remains above -15% and GROCERY_PHARM remains above +19%.

mechanism_narrative: TRANSIT suppression (-1.3% at t-0w) signals ongoing mobility restrictions or low commuter confidence. If TRANSIT remains below -2% for two consecutive weeks, policy-driven access constraints will prevent retail recovery, keeping RETAIL_REC below -12% over the next four weeks.
evidence_refs: fact:TRANSIT has not exceeded -0.4% in four weeks
failure_condition: RETAIL_REC rises above -11% in weeks t+1 and t+2 despite TRANSIT remaining below -2% for both weeks.

mechanism_narrative: PARKS mobility is severely depressed (-19.9%), indicating outdoor recreation avoidance. This signals either weather constraints or behavioral caution. If PARKS remains below -18% over the next week, consumers will shift to indoor retail venues, lifting RETAIL_REC by at least 3 percentage points over the next four weeks.
candidate_trigger: PARKS remains below -18% for week t+1
evidence_refs: fact:PARKS at -19.9%, lowest of all categories
failure_condition: RETAIL_REC does not increase by at least 2 percentage points over the next 28 days, or PARKS improves (rises) above -15%.

mechanism_narrative: RESIDENTIAL elevation (+5.0%) combined with WORKPLACES recovery (-11.7%) and TRANSIT suppression (-1.3%) indicates a hybrid work regime with home-based activity dominance. This three-way interaction will sustain low retail mobility, keeping RETAIL_REC below -12% over the next four weeks.
evidence_refs: fact:All three conditions met at t-0w
failure_condition: RETAIL_REC rises above -10% over the next 28 days while all three conditions (RESIDENTIAL > +4.5%, WORKPLACES > -15%, TRANSIT < -1%) persist.
